7.3. Weak Waves and Evolution🔗

7.3.1. Weak Waves by Galerkin Approximation🔗

Evans §7.2.1–2 (pp. 398–406) defines weak solutions of the second-order hyperbolic Dirichlet problem, constructs finite-dimensional Galerkin approximations, proves their energy bounds, and passes to a weak limit. We work over a Gelfand triple V\hookrightarrow H\hookrightarrow V^*, and the existence theorem takes as hypothesis a bounded projected Galerkin family whose stable trial projections converge strongly to the identity on V.

7.3.1.1. Example: The Concrete Gelfand Triple for Weak Waves🔗

For the wave equation on a bounded domain \Omega\subset\mathbb R^n, the standard Gelfand triple is

V=H^1_0(\Omega)\hookrightarrow H=L^2(\Omega) \hookrightarrow V^*=H^{-1}(\Omega).

Each space carries one part of the wave:

  • V=H^1_0(\Omega) is the energy space. Poincaré's inequality makes \|\nabla u\|_{L^2} an equivalent norm on this space; it measures the potential energy stored in spatial gradients. The zero boundary condition is encoded by the subscript 0. A wave displacement u(t)\in V has finite potential energy.

  • H=L^2(\Omega) is the pivot space. It measures kinetic energy: \|u_t(t)\|_H^2=\int_\Omega|u_t|^2\,dx. The total wave energy is E(t)=\frac12\|u_t(t)\|_{L^2}^2+\frac12\|\nabla u(t)\|_{L^2}^2 for the unit-speed Dirichlet wave equation.

  • V^*=H^{-1}(\Omega) is the dual space. The acceleration u_{tt} lives here: it is a distribution of regularity one spatial derivative below L^2. This is natural because the wave equation u_{tt}=-Au+f has Au=-\Delta u:H^1_0\to H^{-1} as a bounded operator.

The embeddings are dense and continuous, and the pivot space H identifies with its own dual via the Riesz theorem. This identification turns the chain

V\hookrightarrow H\cong H^*\hookrightarrow V^*

into a Gelfand triple. Lions and Magenes (1972, Vol. I, Ch. 1) introduced this framework; Evans (2010, pp. 398–400) adapts it to second-order hyperbolic equations.

With B(u,v)=\int_\Omega\nabla u\cdot\nabla v, the abstract identity u_{tt}+Bu=\ell is exactly the weak Dirichlet wave equation \langle u_{tt},v\rangle+\int_\Omega\nabla u\cdot\nabla v=\langle\ell,v\rangle.

7.3.1.2. The Galerkin Construction for Weak Waves🔗

The construction follows the parabolic case with one difference: the wave equation is second order in time, so both displacement and velocity must be approximated simultaneously, and the energy identity involves kinetic and potential terms rather than a single dissipative form.

At dimension m, one solves the system of 2m ODEs

(u_m''(t),w_k)_H+B(u_m(t),w_k)=\langle\ell(t),w_k\rangle, \quad k=1,\ldots,m,

with projected initial displacement and velocity. For an autonomous symmetric stiffness form B, testing with u_m'(t) gives, almost everywhere,

\frac{d}{dt}\left[\frac12\|u_m'(t)\|_H^2+\frac12B(u_m(t),u_m(t))\right] =\langle\ell(t),u_m'(t)\rangle.

For pivot-valued forcing in L^2(H), Grönwall's inequality, coercivity of B, and uniform projection stability give the bounds \|u_m\|_{L^\infty(V)}+\|u_m'\|_{L^\infty(H)}+\|u_m''\|_{L^2(V^*)}\leq C independently of m. Weak compactness in reflexive Bochner spaces extracts a common limit.

Fix a finite interval a<b and forcing \ell\in L^2(a,b;V^*). A weak wave consists of displacement in L^2(V), velocity in L^2(H), and acceleration in L^2(V^*). Integrated time-derivative identities carry the initial traces, and the spatial equation u_{tt}+B(t)u=\ell holds almost everywhere in V^*.

    Evans's weak solution of the abstract wave equation

    u_tt(t) + B(t)u(t) = ell(t)

    on (a,b), with initial displacement q₀ ∈ V and initial velocity p₀ ∈ H.

The solution concept is stated for the limit object; the construction begins one level down, with a finite-dimensional trial space S_m in which the abstract equation becomes a linear system of ordinary differential equations for the coefficients.

    Existence of the finite-dimensional pivot-mass Galerkin approximation for the weak wave equation.

    This is the coordinate-free counterpart of Evans's coefficient equations in §7.2.2. The ambient form is bounded and strongly measurable in time. The dual forcing is merely Bochner integrable; Evans's f ∈ L²(0,T;L²(U)), embedded into V* through the pivot space, is a special case on a finite interval.

Proof for Theorem 7.66
uses 0

The second-order equation is rewritten as a first-order affine system for displacement and velocity. Finite-dimensional Carathéodory existence applies, and projection to the two state components recovers the two almost-everywhere equations and initial values.

A coefficient trajectory lives in S_m; to compare it with the eventual limit it must be read as an element of the three Bochner spaces in which weak waves live.

✓L∃∀N

For the acceleration realization, assume additionally that the ODE forcing is represented in L^2(a,b;V^*) and that B is strongly measurable almost everywhere and essentially bounded. Under these hypotheses, a finite-dimensional Galerkin trajectory is realized canonically as a displacement in L^2(a,b;V), a velocity in L^2(a,b;H), and an acceleration in L^2(a,b;V^*). The acceleration is the residual projected through a stable trial projection, since the finite system tests only against its own trial space. This projected residual agrees almost everywhere with the coefficient acceleration embedded in V^*.

    Canonical Bochner L²(V*) acceleration associated with a Galerkin trajectory.

    The construction first forms the ambient residual ell - B(·)u in L²(V*) and then precomposes it with the stable trial projection. The pointwise representative theorem below proves that this class is exactly the pivot-embedded coefficient acceleration.

Once realized in Bochner spaces, the Galerkin trajectory satisfies the same two integrated time identities that define a weak wave. The integrated form matters: a boundary value of an L^2 class has no meaning, whereas pairing against a time test \tau with \tau(b)=0 records the initial value unambiguously.

Write J:V\to H for the inclusion, and let q_m,p_m\in S_m be the finite-level initial displacement and velocity. The Galerkin displacement u_m, pivot velocity v_m, and dual acceleration a_m satisfy, for every w\in V and time test \tau with \tau(b)=0,

-\int_a^b(v_m,Jw)_H\tau' =\int_a^b\langle a_m,w\rangle\tau+(Jp_m,Jw)_H\tau(a).

    The pivot velocity and the canonical dual acceleration satisfy the integrated time-derivative identity with the prescribed initial velocity.

    This is the second time identity in Evans's weak-wave formulation. It is again valid for every ambient test v : V; only the separate spatial equation remains projected at the finite-dimensional level.

Proof for Theorem 7.68
uses 0

Pair the coefficient equations with an ambient test and integrate by parts against \tau. The final-time term vanishes because \tau(b)=0; the initial terms are the pairings with Jq_m and Jp_m. Almost-everywhere agreement of the canonical Bochner realizations gives the displayed identities.

The time identities hold against every w\in V, but the spatial equation does not: at finite level it is known only after projecting the test onto S_m. What does survive uniformly is a bound, because the stable projection has norm at most K independently of m.

    Almost-everywhere spatial equation satisfied by a finite-dimensional Galerkin trajectory.

    The acceleration acts on the ambient test v, while the stiffness and forcing act on its trial projection. This is the precise equation that can be passed to the limit when the projections converge strongly to the identity.

Proof for Theorem 7.69
uses 0

The projected dual residual is the forcing minus the stiffness applied to the Galerkin displacement. Boundedness of the stiffness, stability of the trial projection, and the displacement and forcing norms control this residual in L^2(V^*), with constants independent of dimension. Evaluating the projection against a test gives the projected spatial equation.

Passing to the limit is a closedness question in the weak topology. The integrated identities and the equation are linear, so they survive weak convergence once the operator field is essentially bounded.

    Weak sequential/net closure of Evans's weak-wave solution predicate.

    Suppose a family of weak-wave solutions has a common weak limit in the three natural Bochner spaces:

    • displacement in L²(a,b;V),
    • velocity in L²(a,b;H), and
    • acceleration in L²(a,b;V*).

    The acceleration convergence is stated after Riesz transport, matching the Hilbert weak topology used by the compactness theorem. Then the three limit objects again satisfy the weak-wave predicate with the same initial data and forcing.

    The proof follows the Evans limit passage:

    1. bounded linearity of H → V* passes the displacement identity;
    2. fixed space-time testing passes the velocity identity; and
    3. bounded operator-valued multiplication passes B(t)u weakly, so uniqueness of weak limits yields u_tt + B(t)u = ell in L²(V*).
Proof for Theorem 7.70
uses 0

Bounded linear maps pass the displacement identity and the time-test velocity identity to the limit. Bounded operator-valued multiplication passes B(t)u_m weakly, and uniqueness of weak limits identifies the limiting acceleration equation.

Galerkin approximations are not exact weak waves, since their spatial equation is only projected, so closedness alone does not apply to them. The missing ingredient is strong convergence of the projections to the identity on V: pairing weakly convergent residuals with strongly convergent tests P_mw\to w recovers the ambient equation in the limit.

uses 0

The residuals \ell-Bu_m converge weakly in L^2(V^*). Uniform projection stability lifts P_mw\to w to strong convergence on L^2(V) tests. Pairing the bounded weak residuals with those strongly convergent tests identifies the acceleration limit with \ell-Bu.

Combining the uniform bounds with the two limit theorems yields existence.

    Evans, §7.2.3, Theorem 5(i): abstract Galerkin form.

    Assume a bounded projected Galerkin family with the same exact initial displacement q₀ and velocity p₀ at every index. Suppose in addition that estimate (52) has supplied dimension-independent essential bounds

    ‖uₘ(t)‖_V ≤ Cᵤ and ‖uₘ'(t)‖_H ≤ Cᵥ.

    Then the compactness construction produces a weak solution satisfying

    u ∈ L∞(a,b;V) and u_t ∈ L∞(a,b;H),

    with the same almost-everywhere bounds. In concrete divergence-form wave problems, ae_norm_displacementLp_le_of_gelfandWaveEnergy_le and ae_norm_velocityLp_le_of_gelfandWaveEnergy_le supply these two additional hypotheses from the coercive Galerkin energy estimate.

    The proof uses the same common ultrafilter for displacement, velocity, and acceleration. The weak-wave equations are passed to the limit exactly as in exists_of_bounded_projected_galerkin_family, while improvedRegularity_of_weak_L2_limits preserves the closed convex essential norm balls. Thus the regularity conclusion is proved rather than stored as extra data in the definition of a weak solution.

Proof for Theorem 7.72
uses 1

We follow Evans (2010, pp. 405–406) in the abstract Gelfand-triple setting.

Uniform bounds. The assumed energy bounds give \|u_m\|_{L^\infty(V)}+\|u_m'\|_{L^\infty(H)}\leq C, and the accelerations are assumed bounded, \|u_m''\|_{L^2(V^*)}\leq C, both independent of the trial dimension m.

Weak compactness. The spaces L^2(a,b;V), L^2(a,b;H), and L^2(a,b;V^*) are reflexive Banach spaces. The uniform bounds place the Galerkin family in a bounded ball of their product. Reflexive weak compactness, applied simultaneously to the three coordinates, gives weak limits u\in L^2(V), v\in L^2(H), a\in L^2(V^*).

Passing the equation to the limit. Bounded linear time-test functionals pass both integrated identities to the limit, retaining their fixed initial boundary terms. The projected spatial limit theorem Theorem 7.71 supplies the ambient equation by weak–strong testing. Together these give the weak-wave predicate.

Essential supremum bounds. The set of L^2(V) functions satisfying \|u(t)\|_V\leq C almost everywhere is norm-closed and convex, hence weakly closed in L^2(V). The displacement limit belongs to that same set. The identical argument in L^2(H) preserves the velocity bound.

In practice the Galerkin data are projections q_m=P_mq_0 and p_m=P_mp_0 of the exact data, so they vary with m. Strong convergence of the projected data is enough to pass the initial boundary terms of the integrated identities to the limit.

    Evans's projected Galerkin limit passage with convergent approximate initial data.

    Unlike of_projected_galerkin_weak_limits, the finite-dimensional displacement and velocity may start from trial-space projections depending on the Galerkin index. Strong convergence of those initial values identifies the two endpoint terms in the limiting weak-wave equations.

Proof for Theorem 7.73
uses 1

Pass the time integrals through weak convergence. Strong convergence of q_m and p_m gives convergence of both initial boundary pairings against each fixed test. The projected spatial limit theorem Theorem 7.71 supplies the remaining ambient equation under the same measurable, essentially bounded coefficient hypothesis.

The displacement of a weak wave is only an L^2(V) class, so u(t) has no meaning at an individual time. The integrated displacement identity nevertheless says that u has a weak time derivative in V^*, namely the embedded velocity, which is enough regularity to select a continuous pivot-valued representative. The energy-uniqueness argument evaluates that representative at a terminal time \sigma.

    The weak displacement has a strongly continuous pivot-space representative with the prescribed initial trace.

    This is the first regularity consequence of the weak-wave definition. It is obtained from the already proved finite-interval Lions-Magenes theorem, applied to the integrated equation u_t = velocity. No endpoint value of the Lp V representative is evaluated.

Proof for Theorem 7.74
uses 0

Apply the finite-interval continuous-representative theorem to the integrated displacement equation, with the pivot velocity embedded into V^* as its weak time derivative. This gives a continuous pivot-space representative agreeing almost everywhere with Ju. The initial boundary term identifies its value at the lower endpoint with Jq_0.

7.3.2. Energy Uniqueness🔗

Uniqueness of weak waves (Evans §7.2.2) follows by testing the homogeneous equation against a backward time primitive and repeating the estimate on a finite partition of the time interval. The argument here runs over an abstract Gelfand triple.

Theorem 7.76
Loading preview
Reverse dependency preview content is loaded from the rendered-fragment cache.
✓L∃∀N

For a<b and a terminal time \sigma\in[a,b], set W_\sigma(t)=\int_t^\sigma u(r)\,dr. Let a homogeneous weak wave have zero initial displacement and velocity at a. Assume its principal form A is symmetric, coercive with constant c>0, and absolutely continuous in time, with coefficient derivative bound L_A and pivot-to-energy lower-order bound L_R\geq0. Under the scalar integrability hypotheses for the backward-energy identity, it satisfies

\frac12\|u(\sigma)\|_H^2+\frac c2\|W_\sigma(a)\|_V^2 \leq \frac{L_A}{2}\int_a^\sigma\|W_\sigma(t)\|_V^2\,dt +\frac{L_R}{2}\int_a^\sigma \bigl(\|u(t)\|_H^2+\|W_\sigma(t)\|_V^2\bigr)\,dt.

Here u(\sigma) denotes the continuous pivot-space displacement representative. Zero initial data remove the initial boundary terms.

          LR * ‖T.inclusion x‖ * ‖y‖) :

    Evans's backward estimate for a fixed canonical displacement evolution.

    The preceding theorem constructs an evolution together with the estimate. Canonical-representative uniqueness shows that the endpoint norm is independent of that construction, so the same inequality holds for any ContinuousPivotEvolutionOn representing the displacement. This nonexistential form is the one used by the Grönwall and interval-restart arguments.

Proof for Theorem 7.75
uses 0

The weak equation is tested against a backward time primitive. Integration by parts exposes the endpoint pivot norm and the principal energy. Coercivity controls the primitive, while the coefficient derivative and lower-order form are estimated by their stated quadratic bounds.

By itself the estimate is not yet a Grönwall inequality, because W_\sigma(t)=W_\sigma(a)-W_t(a) ties the right-hand side to the endpoint quantity \|W_\sigma(a)\|_V with a coefficient of order \sigma-a. On an interval short enough for that coefficient to be absorbed into the left-hand side, Grönwall's inequality gives u=0 up to \sigma.

    Finite restart of the short-interval Evans uniqueness argument.

    The points τ 0, …, τ N form an ordered finite partition of [a,b]. Each adjacent interval is short enough for estimate (40), and hcover records that these intervals cover the full time domain. Induction carries both zero traces from one partition point to the next; the velocity trace is recovered from the vanishing displacement by weak derivative uniqueness.

    The partition is explicit so this theorem is useful beyond uniform meshes: applications may refine only where coefficient bounds require it.

Proof for Theorem 7.76
uses 1

The backward estimate and Grönwall argument give vanishing on the first short interval. The zero displacement and velocity traces at its right endpoint restart the same argument on the next interval. Finite induction covers the whole interval.

Uniqueness for general data follows from the homogeneous zero-data case by subtraction, which is pure linear algebra on the weak-wave predicate.

Suppose every homogeneous zero-data weak wave satisfies (w,w_t,w_{tt})=(0,0,0). If u_1 and u_2 have the same operator, forcing, displacement trace, and velocity trace, then their difference is such a homogeneous solution, hence

u_1=u_2,\qquad (u_1)_t=(u_2)_t,\qquad (u_1)_{tt}=(u_2)_{tt}.

    Evans's reduction of uniqueness to the homogeneous zero-data problem.

    Once every weak solution with zero forcing and zero initial traces is known to vanish, subtraction identifies the displacement, velocity, and acceleration of any two solutions with the same data. The analytic content of Theorem 4 is therefore isolated in hhomogeneous; this theorem performs the exact linearity argument and no regularity shortcut.

Proof for Theorem 7.77
uses 0

Subtract the two weak formulations. Linearity cancels the common forcing and initial traces, so the difference is a homogeneous zero-data weak wave. Applying homogeneous uniqueness to its displacement, velocity, and acceleration gives equality of the corresponding components.

Of the three scalar integrability conditions in the backward estimate, two come from measurability and the coefficient bounds: the coefficient derivative and lower-order pairings along u and W_\sigma. For the difference of two solutions, the homogeneous weak equation identifies B(u,W_\sigma) with the negative acceleration pairing; A=B-R then gives integrability of the principal pairing.

used by 0✓L∃∀N

In the real Hilbert Gelfand-triple setting, write J:V\hookrightarrow H for the inclusion and assume B=A+R on [a,b]. Require A to be absolutely continuous in operator norm, with A'(t)=\dot A(t) for almost every t\in(a,b]. Both \dot A and R must be almost everywhere strongly measurable as operator-valued maps. For every t\in[a,b], assume A(t) is symmetric and, for all v,w\in V,

\kappa\|v\|_V^2\leq A(t)(v,v),\qquad |\dot A(t)(v,v)|\leq L_A\|v\|_V^2,\qquad |R(t)(v,w)|\leq L_R\|Jv\|_H\|w\|_V,

where \kappa>0 and L_A,L_R\geq0. Two weak waves for this operator with equal forcing and initial traces then satisfy

u_1=u_2\ \text{in }L^2(a,b;V),\qquad v_1=v_2\ \text{in }L^2(a,b;H),\qquad a_1=a_2\ \text{in }L^2(a,b;V^*).

The scalar integrability conditions inside the backward-energy identity are derived from the L^2 trajectories, the coefficient bounds, and the weak equation.

    Evans, §7.2.2 weak-wave uniqueness with coefficient-level assumptions.

    Unlike eq_of_evans_coefficients, this theorem has no scalar IntervalIntegrable hypotheses. The L² solution types and homogeneous weak equation provide integrability of B(u,v), hence of A(u,v)=B(u,v)-R(u,v). Strong measurability is needed only for Adot and R, the two fields not already represented by the weak equation. In concrete divergence form it follows from measurability of the coefficient fields. hAdotBound follows from uniform bounds on the time derivative of the principal coefficients. hRBound puts the H norm on the solution slot, so it follows from uniform bounds on c, b and div b after a spatial integration by parts; bounds on b alone do not give it.

Proof for Theorem 7.78
uses 1

Subtract the two waves, construct a sufficiently fine uniform finite partition, apply the backward-energy estimate on each cell, restart from the zero endpoint traces, and identify the vanishing continuous representative with all three Bochner classes.

7.3.3. Higher Regularity and Compatibility🔗

Evans §7.2.3 proves higher regularity for the autonomous second-order hyperbolic Dirichlet problem. We split his argument into compatibility traces, differentiated Galerkin chains, weak-limit identification, and elliptic lifting, which shows which initial traces and spatial estimates each additional derivative needs.

7.3.3.1. Compatibility and Differentiated Galerkin Chains🔗

Differentiating the wave equation in time creates a finite hierarchy of wave problems. Compatibility conditions supply the initial data for every level, and one common compactness extraction is needed so that adjacent weak limits remain derivatives of each other.

✓L∃∀N

The data consist of a finite Sobolev time jet, initial displacement and velocity of matching spatial orders, and the formal initial derivatives

g_0=g,\qquad g_1=h,\qquad g_{k+2}=\partial_t^k f(0)-Bg_k.

Compatibility requires each g_k to lie in the spatial space prescribed for \partial_t^ku(0), to have the homogeneous Dirichlet trace when required, and to satisfy this recurrence. Compatibility thus fixes both the regularity budget and the boundary values of the formal derivatives.

    Concrete m-th order compatibility for an Evans wave problem.

    The endpoint traces are generated from the verified forcing jet. Each Sobolev-scale application in the recurrence is certified against the same weak operator A.

At order m=1, consider u_{tt}-\Delta u=f with u(0)=g and u_t(0)=h. Evaluating the equation at time zero gives the first nontrivial compatibility value

u_{tt}(0)=f(0)+\Delta g.

Higher regularity requires this expression to lie in the space prescribed for the second time derivative and to satisfy the corresponding boundary compatibility. The recursive formal data encode this same calculation at every later order.

A Sobolev time jet on a nontrivial interval admits coherent dual-valued representatives F_0,\ldots,F_m, all but the last absolutely continuous, such that

\partial_tF_k=F_{k+1}\quad\text{for almost every }t, \qquad 0\leq k<m.

Each representative agrees almost everywhere with the Dirichlet load of the matching jet entry, so later Galerkin systems use one compatible chain rather than unrelated representatives of the weak derivatives.

Proof for Theorem 7.80
uses 0

Start with a representative of the highest weak time derivative. Descend through the jet, choosing at each level the Sobolev representative whose weak derivative is the representative already fixed one level above. The Sobolev time-derivative identities hold almost everywhere, and the canonical embeddings into the dual energy space preserve both those identities and the prescribed Bochner integrability.

The nonterminal forcing representatives have canonical initial traces F_k(0) for 0\leq k<m. These are the values used in the compatibility recurrence. The highest forcing derivative needs only its Bochner integrability.

Compatible wave data determine the initial displacement g_k and velocity g_{k+1} of each differentiated problem, for 0\leq k\leq m. Adjacent levels satisfy the formal acceleration relation

Proof for Theorem 7.81
uses 0

Embed each formal compatibility value g_k into the common ambient energy space and pair adjacent values as displacement and velocity. The compatibility recurrence g_{k+2}=F_k(0)-Bg_k rearranges to the required initial acceleration equation. Coherence of the forcing representatives ensures that all levels use the same time-zero data rather than independent choices.

Each differentiated problem could be solved by the Galerkin method for weak waves, but separate compactness extractions would produce limits with no relation to one another.

    Evans Section 7.2.3: construction through compactness.

    The assumptions are the basis-free compatibility equations for the finite ambient initial jet, Ritz orthogonality of the trial projections, and the common structural hypotheses used in the wave-energy estimate. The Galerkin trajectories and all three bounded approximation families are constructed in the proof.

Theorem 7.66
Loading preview
Proof dependency preview content is loaded from the rendered-fragment cache.

Finite-dimensional differentiated trajectories are built first. Uniform energy bounds provide bounded families at every level. One common compactness extraction passes all equations and adjacent derivative identities to the limit, including the convergent projected initial values.

Symmetry of B enters the chain theorem through the Ritz property of the projected initial data and through the energy identity behind the uniform bounds. When B=A+R has a nonsymmetric remainder, the energy bounds can still be run on the symmetric coercive part A, but Ritz orthogonality must be imposed for the full operator.

Let the autonomous operator split as B=A+R, with A symmetric and coercive and with a possibly nonsymmetric remainder satisfying

|R(v,w)|\leq L_R\|v\|_V\|Jw\|_H.

In addition to compatible data, stable dense trial projections, and a uniform forcing budget, assume full-operator Ritz orthogonality:

(A+R)(q-P_kq,w)=0\qquad\text{for every }w\in S_k,

for each initial jet entry q used in the adjacent compatibility recurrence. Here P_k is the restriction of the stable pivot projection to V. This condition is separate from stability and density, and orthogonality for A alone does not imply it. Under these hypotheses, the theorem constructs a common finite chain of weak-wave limits for B, retaining every adjacent time-derivative identity.

    Evans Section 7.2.3: differentiated Galerkin limit with bounded nonsymmetric lower-order terms.

    Let the autonomous wave operator split as B = A + R. The principal part A is symmetric and coercive on the energy space, while R is allowed to be nonsymmetric and is controlled in the mixed V x H norm. Stable dense trial projections, compatible ambient initial data, a coherent forcing chain, and the uniform forcing budget generate a finite chain of ambient weak-wave solutions for the full operator A + R, provided hRitz holds:

    (A + R) (q r.succ - P_k (q r.succ)) w = 0

    for every trial level k, adjacent jet index r, and test w in that trial space. Here P_k is the restriction of the stable pivot projection to V. This full-operator condition is separate from stability and density.

    All finite-dimensional trajectories, their uniform bounds, and their common weak limit are constructed in the proof. In particular, no limiting weak wave or higher-regularity conclusion is included among the hypotheses.

Proof for Theorem 7.83
uses 0

Full-operator Ritz orthogonality makes the projected initial jet satisfy the differentiated finite-dimensional equations. The uniform energy bounds take A as the coercive symmetric energy form. The mixed estimate on R absorbs the remainder in that energy estimate, at the cost of a larger exponential rate. Apply the common finite-chain compactness extraction to all differentiated Galerkin trajectories at once; weak convergence passes both the A and R terms to the limit and preserves every adjacent time-derivative identity.

7.3.3.2. Nonsymmetric Elliptic Lifting🔗

Time differentiation controls the temporal jet. Spatial derivatives are recovered by reading the wave equation at almost every time as an elliptic problem. A Gårding shift gives coercivity for lower-order nonsymmetric terms, and the elliptic regularity theory supplies the two-spatial-derivative lift.

uses 1used by 0✓L∃∀N

If the principal form is coercive and the lower-order remainder obeys the mixed V\times H bound, Young's inequality gives the exact Gårding loss

\frac c2\|v\|_V^2 \leq (A+R)(v,v)+\frac{L_R^2}{2c}\|Jv\|_H^2.

Adding this canonical pivot-mass shift makes the full, possibly nonsymmetric operator coercive, and identifies an unshifted weak solution with the shifted Lax–Milgram solution after correcting the load. This is an abstract Gelfand-triple analogue of the elliptic Gårding construction.

    An unshifted weak solution is exactly the Lax-Milgram solution of the canonically shifted problem with the corrected load

    ell + μ J*J u.

    Nonsymmetric elliptic lifting uses this identity. It is proved from the original weak equation and shifted coercivity.

Proof for Theorem 7.84
uses 0

The remainder estimate and Young's inequality give |R(v,v)|\leq \frac c2\|v\|_V^2+ \frac{L_R^2}{2c}\|Jv\|_H^2. Subtract this loss from the coercive lower bound for A(v,v) to obtain the displayed Gårding inequality. Adding the pivot-mass term therefore makes the shifted form coercive. Moving the same mass term to the load shows that an unshifted weak solution solves the shifted Lax–Milgram problem.

The Gårding shift is abstract; its payoff comes from the concrete divergence-form operator, for which the shifted problem is coercive and the elliptic regularity theory applies.

Let n>0 and let the domain carry the operational C2BoundaryAtlas. Assume uniformly elliptic W^{1,\infty} principal coefficients with global C^1 representatives and bounded first- and zeroth-order coefficients. The Gårding-shifted homogeneous Dirichlet solver has a bounded L^2\to H^2 lift. Every unshifted weak solution u\in H^1_0(\Omega) with f\in L^2(\Omega) therefore has an H^2 representative satisfying

\|u\|_{H^2}\leq C\bigl(\|f\|_{L^2}+|\mu|\,\|u\|_{L^2}\bigr).

This supplies the order-two elliptic step in Evans's wave regularity argument, for a full operator that need not be symmetric.

    Usable nonsymmetric form of Evans, §7.2.3 (59)-(60).

    If u solves the unshifted full equation L u = f, then u has a global H² representative satisfying

    ‖u‖_{H²} <= C (‖f‖_{L²} + |μ| ‖u‖_{L²}),

    where μ is the Gårding shift and C is the operator norm of the shifted full L² -> H² solver constructed above.

Proof for Theorem 7.85
uses 0

Rewrite the unshifted equation as the coercive shifted problem with corrected load f+\mu u. Lax–Milgram uniqueness identifies the given weak solution with the shifted solver. Apply the global divergence-form H^2 regularity operator to that load and use its norm bound; the triangle inequality yields the displayed dependence on \|f\|_{L^2} and |\mu|\|u\|_{L^2}.

Two derivatives at a time is the natural step of elliptic regularity, and iterating it requires the same shifted solver to map H^k loads to H^{k+2} solutions for every k. The load at level k is f+\mu u with u already controlled in H^k, which is why the estimate takes the form of a two-step recurrence.

used by 0✓L∃∀N

Retain the domain, uniform ellipticity, and homogeneous Dirichlet hypotheses of the order-two lift. At order k, assume principal coefficients in W^{k+1,\infty} with global C^{k+1} representatives, lower-order coefficients in W^{k,\infty}, and an operational boundary atlas whose charts are C^{k+2} and whose inverse charts are C^{k+1}. The shifted solver is then bounded from H^k to H^{k+2}. An unshifted weak solution with an already identified H^k representative receives an H^{k+2} lift, with a bound in terms of the H^k forcing and solution norms.

Proof for Theorem 7.86
uses 0

As in the order-two case, shift the equation and correct the load by the pivot-mass term. The arbitrary-order elliptic bootstrap maps an H^k load to an H^{k+2} solution under the coefficient and boundary hypotheses. Uniqueness identifies this lift with the original weak solution, and boundedness of the solver gives the two-step norm estimate.

7.3.3.3. Identifying the Regular Wave🔗

The differentiated weak limits are derivatives of one solution, and elliptic lifting applies to its spatial slices. Here the time-regularity and spatial-regularity arguments meet.

uses 1used by 0✓L∃∀N

For an autonomous operator, suppose the original limit is a weak wave, the forcing has a weak time derivative, and the original and differentiated Galerkin families have common weak limits with their exact derivative links. The theorem identifies u_t, u_{tt}, and a third weak time derivative. Uniform essential bounds on the differentiated families pass to the limit.

    Evans, §7.2.3, Theorem 5(ii): identification of the differentiated Galerkin limits.

    Suppose one common filter gives weak limits for an original Galerkin family and its differentiated family. The exact finite-dimensional identities

    J (duₘ) = velocityₘ,

    J* (dvelocityₘ) = accelerationₘ

    then survive weak convergence. If the coefficient derivative identity d uₘ/dt = duₘ is also retained in the identity Gelfand triple, the limit du is the V-valued weak derivative of u.

    Uniform essential bounds on duₘ in V and dvelocityₘ in H pass to the same limits by weak closedness of the almost-everywhere norm balls. Finally, for an autonomous operator and weakly differentiable forcing, the theorem constructs u_{ttt} in L²(a,b;V*).

    This is the compactness/identification step that cannot be justified by extracting unrelated subnets for the original and differentiated systems.

Proof for Theorem 7.87
uses 0

Test the Galerkin identity relating each trajectory to its time derivative against smooth compactly supported time functions. Weak convergence passes that distributional identity to the paired limits, identifying the latter as successive weak derivatives of one function. Then differentiate u_{tt}=\ell-Bu: autonomy gives u_{ttt}=\partial_t\ell-Bu_t in L^2(V^*). The almost-everywhere norm-bound sets are closed and convex in L^2, so their weak closedness preserves the uniform essential bounds.

For the pivot space H=L^2(\Omega), the paired-limit theorem identifies the dual-valued acceleration with the pivot image of an L^2(\Omega)-valued class and preserves its essential spatial L^2 bound. That is the input the elliptic lift needs at almost every time.

Let n>0 and let the domain carry the operational C2BoundaryAtlas. Assume uniformly elliptic W^{1,\infty} principal coefficients with global C^1 representatives. For a time-L^2 trajectory in H^1_0(\Omega) satisfying the weak wave equation with spatial L^2 forcing and acceleration, essential bounds on those two spatial norms give an essentially bounded H^2 lift. The elliptic solver's operator norm gives the quantitative estimate.

    Evans, §7.2.3: the elliptic step in Theorem 5(ii).

    Assume the divergence-form weak wave identity holds almost everywhere in time and that both f(t) and u_{tt}(t) are essentially bounded in L²(Omega). On a domain carrying the operational C2BoundaryAtlas, assume uniformly elliptic W¹,∞ principal coefficients with global C¹ representatives. The wave trajectory then has a canonical L∞_t H²_x representative. Constructing the atlas from an ordinary geometric C² boundary is not part of this theorem.

    The pointwise estimate retained by the theorem is

    ‖u(t)‖_{H²} ≤ ‖S₂‖ (C_f + C_tt),

    where S₂ : L²(Omega) → H²(Omega) is the global elliptic solution operator. This is the operator form of Evans's estimates (59)-(60). In particular, the constant is independent of the Galerkin dimension and of time.

Proof for Theorem 7.88
uses 0

For almost every time, rewrite the wave equation as the elliptic problem Bu(t)=f(t)-u_{tt}(t). The global elliptic regularity solver supplies an H^2 representative of that spatial slice, and uniqueness identifies it with u(t). Measurability of the bounded solver assembles these slices into a Bochner representative, while the operator norm and the two essential L^2 bounds give the essential-supremum estimate.

Assembling the pieces gives the existence theorem. Symmetry of the spatial operator is assumed because the chain theorem invoked is the symmetric one.

Under the explicit compatibility, stable-density, coercivity, Ritz, and elliptic-lifting hypotheses, and assuming the spatial operator is symmetric, there exists a weak wave with the prescribed initial data and an essentially bounded Sobolev time jet of order m+1 whose head agrees almost everywhere with the displacement and whose first time derivative is the velocity. For a nonsymmetric operator, the corresponding steps are the nonsymmetric Galerkin chain and the higher-order lift.

Proof for Theorem 7.90
uses 0

Each assumed level estimate bounds one nonnegative summand almost everywhere. Intersect the finitely many full-measure sets so that all bounds hold simultaneously, then sum them pointwise. Monotonicity of the essential supremum transfers this finite pointwise sum to the left-hand side, and the assumed upper bound for the sum of level constants produces the single factor C multiplying the data budget.

uses 1used by 0✓L∃∀N

Let M_k be the recursively defined majorant obtained from the two top differentiated energy bounds and an assumed two-step spatial recurrence, after factoring out the data budget B. The recurrence bounds the H^{k+2} entry \partial_t^{m-1-k}u(t) of the norm sum by the forcing, the H^k entry \partial_t^{m+1-k}u(t), and a shift term in the H^{k+1} entry \partial_t^{m-k}u(t). The resulting bound is

\operatorname*{ess\,sup}_{t\in(t_0,t_1)} \sum_{k=0}^{m+1}\|\partial_t^ku(t)\|_{H^{m+1-k}} \leq \left(\sum_{k=0}^{m+1}M_k\right)B.

Here B is the forcing and initial-data budget in the preceding estimate. Both starting bounds and the recurrence are hypotheses, and the proof propagates them through the finite derivative hierarchy. The recurrence has a different shape from the higher-order lift, whose shift term falls on the level being solved for rather than on the neighbouring one.

Proof for Theorem 7.91
uses 0

Begin with the two highest time-derivative bounds. Strong induction descends through the Sobolev levels: at each step, the assumed recurrence controls the next spatial norm from the forcing at that level and the two already controlled higher time derivatives. This proves the recursive majorant M_k for every level. The finite assembly theorem then sums these almost-everywhere estimates into the stated essential-supremum bound.

7.3.4. Strongly Continuous Semigroups🔗

For the homogeneous wave equation u_{tt}+Au=0, set U(t)=(u(t),u_t(t)) in the energy space H^1_0\times L^2 and formally write U_t=\mathcal GU with \mathcal G(u,v)=(v,-Au). When \mathcal G generates a strongly continuous group, its positive-time restriction is a semigroup and T(t)U(0) is the wave evolution. The generator domain records the additional regularity needed to interpret \mathcal GU.

A strongly continuous semigroup consists of bounded linear evolution operators T(t) for nonnegative time, with T(0)=I, T(s+t)=T(s)T(t), and a continuous orbit t\mapsto T(t)x for every vector x. This definition requires only a real normed space; completeness enters when the orbits are integrated.

Proof for Theorem 7.95
uses 0

If Ax is the strong derivative of T(h)x at zero, the semigroup law rewrites the difference quotient at T(t)x as T(t) applied to the difference quotient at x. Continuity and linearity of T(t) pass the limit through, giving generator value T(t)Ax and hence T(t)x\in D(A).

Invariance of D(A) means the operators T(t) can be restricted to it.

Proof for Theorem 7.97
uses 1

The difference quotient at T(t)x is, by the semigroup law, T(t) applied to the difference quotient at x. Passing to the strong limit through the bounded linear operator T(t) gives A(T(t)x)=T(t)Ax.

Commutation gives a right derivative at every nonnegative time, and on a Banach space integration upgrades it to an ordinary derivative at positive times.

Every orbit starting in the generator domain solves the abstract homogeneous Cauchy problem. At time zero the derivative is taken within [0,\infty). This one-sided statement holds on a normed space. Proof for Theorem 7.98
uses 1

At zero the generator definition gives the right derivative. The semigroup law transports it to every nonnegative time, and strong continuity makes s\mapsto T(s)Ax continuous. On a Banach space, the fundamental theorem for right derivatives gives T(s)x=x+\int_0^sT(r)Ax\,dr. Near a positive time, the orbit therefore agrees with a differentiable Bochner primitive. Its ordinary derivative is T(t)Ax, continuous in t by strong continuity.

The C^1 claim also requires the derivative t\mapsto T(t)Ax to be continuous, and this holds without completeness.

Proof for Theorem 7.99
uses 1

Generator commutation rewrites the map as the ordinary semigroup orbit of Ax. Strong continuity of the semigroup then gives continuity directly.

How large is D(A)? For a general unbounded operator the domain could be small, but the averages \varepsilon^{-1}\int_0^\varepsilon T(s)x\,ds always belong to it. Since the averages converge to x, the domain is dense; the Bochner integral is where completeness of X enters.

Proof for Theorem 7.100
uses 0

Average the orbit over [0,\varepsilon] and divide by \varepsilon. The semigroup law computes the generator of this average from its endpoint difference, so each average lies in D(A). Strong continuity at zero makes the averages converge to the original vector, proving density.

Density is complemented by closedness: even though A need not be bounded, its graph is closed.

    The infinitesimal generator of a strongly continuous semigroup is closed.

Proof for Theorem 7.101
uses 0

Suppose x_n\to x and Ax_n\to y. Integrating the orbit derivative gives T(t)x_n-x_n=\int_0^tT(s)Ax_n\,ds. Continuity of T(s) and Bochner integration passes this identity to the limit. Dividing by t and sending t\downarrow0 shows that x\in D(A) and Ax=y.

The resolvent is obtained directly as a Laplace transform of the semigroup, without spectral theory. Under the contraction hypothesis, \lVert e^{-\lambda t}T(t)x\rVert\le e^{-\lambda t}\lVert x\rVert makes the weighted orbit Bochner integrable on (0,\infty) for every \lambda>0, so the transform defines an operator.

The Laplace operator maps X into D(A) and is the two-sided inverse of \lambda-A:

R_\lambda(\lambda-A)x=x\quad(x\in D(A)),

(\lambda-A)R_\lambda y=y\quad(y\in X).

In particular, every positive \lambda lies in the resolvent set in the concrete sense that \lambda-A maps the generator domain bijectively onto X.

Proof for Theorem 7.104
uses 0

For x\in D(A), differentiate e^{-\lambda t}T(t)x and integrate from zero to infinity; exponential decay removes the boundary term at infinity and gives R_\lambda(\lambda-A)x=x. Applying the same integrated difference-quotient calculation to arbitrary y shows R_\lambda y\in D(A) and (\lambda-A)R_\lambda y=y. The two identities give bijectivity.

These results are the generator and resolvent half of Evans §7.4. The converse, the Hille–Yosida theorem, constructs a contraction semigroup from the resolvent estimates; the Dirichlet heat semigroup and the autonomous wave semigroup are generated this way.

7.3.4.1. Nonlinear evolution from a convex energy🔗

A proper lower semicontinuous convex energy I:H\to(-\infty,+\infty] on a real Hilbert space can also generate an evolution. Its subdifferential replaces a linear generator:

u'(t)+\partial I(u(t))\ni0.

The energy may be infinite outside its effective domain and need not be differentiable. The construction first solves the weak evolution for initial values in D=\operatorname{dom}\partial I. Contraction then extends the solution maps to \overline D, including initial values where a subgradient is not supplied.

Theorem 6.5.1
Loading preview
Reverse dependency preview content is loaded from the rendered-fragment cache.
✓L∃∀N

Let H be a real Hilbert space, I:H\to(-\infty,+\infty] proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex, and x_0\in D=\operatorname{dom}\partial I. There is a continuous trajectory u:[0,\infty)\to H with u(0)=x_0 and a Bochner velocity g\in L^\infty((0,\infty);H) such that

u'=g\quad\text{in distributions},\qquad -g(t)\in\partial I(u(t))\quad\text{for almost every }t>0.

The trajectory is unique in this continuous weak class, and the velocity is unique almost everywhere. Every u(t) belongs to D. If p_0 is the least-norm element of \partial I(x_0), then

\|u(t)-u(s)\|\le\|p_0\||t-s|,\qquad \|g(t)\|\le\|p_0\|\quad\text{for almost every }t>0.

No density of D or separability of H is required.

    Global existence and uniqueness of the weak subgradient flow from x₀ in the subdifferential domain. With p the least-norm element of ∂I(x₀), there is a weak flow (u, g) with u(0) = x₀ that is ‖p‖-Lipschitz on [0, ∞), has ‖g‖ ≤ ‖p‖ and u' = g almost everywhere, stays in the subdifferential domain, is absolutely continuous on every [0, T], and satisfies ‖u_λ(t) - u(t)‖² ≤ (λ/2) t ‖p‖². The Yosida flows converge to u uniformly on every [0, T], and every weak flow from x₀ equals u on [0, ∞) with velocity equal to g almost everywhere.

Proof for Theorem 7.105
uses 0

The Yosida approximations have a common speed bound supplied by an initial subgradient and converge uniformly on each bounded time interval. Their limit has a weak velocity satisfying the subgradient inclusion; countable exhaustion of the positive half-line gives one global velocity. Choosing the least-norm initial subgradient sharpens the speed bound. Monotonicity gives contraction between weak trajectories, hence uniqueness for equal initial data; uniqueness of the weak derivative identifies their velocities almost everywhere.

Definition 7.92

uses 0used by 0✓L∃∀N

Let H be a real Hilbert space and I:H\to(-\infty,+\infty] be proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex. There is a unique jointly continuous flow S:[0,\infty)\times\overline{\operatorname{dom}\partial I} \to\overline{\operatorname{dom}\partial I} which is contractive and agrees with every weak subgradient trajectory starting in \operatorname{dom}\partial I. In particular,

S(0)x=x,\qquad S(s+t)x=S(s)(S(t)x),\qquad \|S(t)x-S(t)y\|\le\|x-y\|.

For initial values in the closure the orbit is continuous and contractive; the weak velocity and the subgradient inclusion are part of the domain theorem for initial values in \operatorname{dom}\partial I.

    A proper, convex, lower semicontinuous energy on a real Hilbert space gives a unique strongly continuous nonlinear contraction semigroup on the closed subdifferential domain that agrees with all original-domain weak trajectories.

Proof for Theorem 7.106
uses 1

The global weak subgradient-flow theorem gives unique trajectories on D. Monotonicity of the subdifferential makes the distance between two trajectories nonincreasing. At each fixed time the solution map is therefore 1-Lipschitz, so it extends uniquely from the dense set D to the complete space \overline D. The identity and composition laws pass to the closure by continuity. Contraction controls changes of initial data uniformly in time, while continuity of each orbit controls changes of time; together they give joint continuity. Any other flow agreeing on D agrees everywhere by density.

The nonlinear Dirichlet diffusion application identifies a concrete energy's subdifferential with a spatial differential operator. That identification is what turns this abstract evolution into a PDE with boundary data.
